We developed a static deterministic model that explicitly accounted for the varied risks for RSV admission by birth month and chronological age in month and projected the annual RSV-associated ALRI hospital admissions and RSV-attributable deaths under two scenarios: a no-implementation scenario that assumed the same hospital admission and mortality rates to the 2019 baseline, and a June-2025 product use scenario that was based on country-level implementation status of novel RSV prophylactic products as of June 2025; the two scenarios were then compared to estimate the impact of the current implementation of novel prophylactic products. We further calculated the ratio of RSV-attributable deaths between the highest and lowest burden quintiles (Q5-Q1 ratio) to assess inequality under the two scenarios. Findings At baseline, the African Region had the highest incidence of RSV-associated ALRI (117.4 per 1000 person-years, 95% uncertainty range, UR: 60.0–229.8) and highest RSV-attributable mortality rate (0.97 per 1000 person-years, 95% UR: 0.76–1.31) while having the lowest RSV-associated ALRI hospital admission rate (12.6 per 1000 person-years; 95% UR: 7.5–21.3); the Eastern Mediterranean Region had the highest hospital admission rate (29.9 per 1000 person-years, 95% UR: 14.2–63.2). The regional variations in incidence, hospital admission, and mortality rates persisted when further stratifying the above estimates by country income level. As of June 2025, nirsevimab and maternal RSVpreF had been licensed in 54 and 64 countries, respectively, with 16 and 12 countries introducing them into their national immunisation programmes. A total of 4,641,000 doses of nirsevimab and 1,955,000 doses of RSVPreF were estimated to be administered annually under the June-2025 product use scenario globally. Administration of both products was projected to jointly avert 91,000 (95% UR: 75,000–118,000) RSV-associated ALRI hospital admissions and 300 (95% UR: 210–470) RSV-attributable deaths in infants annually, corresponding to 3.7% (95% UR: 2.7–4.9) and 0.4% (95% UR: 0.3–0.7) of the global admissions and deaths, respectively. Approximately 90% of averted hospital admissions and over 70% of averted deaths in infants occurred in high-income countries (81,000 [95% UR: 66,000–108,000] and 220 [95% UR: 140–390], respectively), corresponding to reductions of 33.2% (95% UR 31.0–35.9) and 29.1% (95% UR 22.6–35.2); by contrast, the relative reduction of admissions and deaths in middle-income countries was less than 5%, and no reduction was expected in low-income countries. Globally, substantial inequality was observed in the RSV-attributable overall mortality burden under the no-implementation scenario, with the Q5-Q1 ratio of RSV-attributable deaths estimated at 18.3 (95% UR: 11.7–27.5). The June-2025 product use scenario was associated with a possible slight increase in global inequality, with the Q5-Q1 ratio rising to 20.8 (95% UR: 13.0–31.7). Interpretation The global RSV burden in 2019 varied substantially by region and income level, with the African Region exhibiting the highest incidence and mortality but the lowest hospitalisation rates. The current implementation of novel RSV prophylactic products, characterised by widespread licensing and use in high-income countries and lack of availability in LMICs, particularly the African Region, is projected to yield only modest reductions in the global infant RSV disease burden. Critically, inequitable access to these products may exacerbate existing inequalities in RSV mortality burden. These findings underscore the urgent need for targeted strategies to accelerate the introduction and scale-up of infant RSV immunisation programmes in LMICs. Funding World Health Organization and National Natural Science Foundation of China (82473692).
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是婴幼儿急性下呼吸道感染(ALRI)的主要病因,低收入和中等收入国家(LMICs)承担了不成比例的高负担。尽管新型RSV预防产品,包括长效单克隆抗体和母体RSVpreF,正在高收入国家推出以保护一般婴幼儿群体,但在LMICs的实施预计要到2028年,这可能会加剧健康不平等。我们旨在评估在实施这些干预措施前后的婴幼儿RSV疾病负担的区域不平等。方法:我们重新分析了2019年按世界卫生组织地区和世界银行收入分类的全球RSV疾病负担数据集,使用广义线性混合效应模型。我们开发了一个静态确定性模型,明确考虑了出生月份和月龄对RSV入院风险的差异,并在两种情景下预测了每年与RSV相关的ALRI住院人数和RSV归因死亡人数:一种是没有实施的情景,假设住院率和RSV归因死亡率与2019年的基线相同;另一种是2025年6月产品使用情景,基于2025年6月各国新型RSV预防产品的实施状态。然后比较这两种情景,以估计当前新型预防产品的实施影响。我们进一步计算了在两种情景下最高和最低负担五分位数(Q5-Q1比值)之间的RSV归因死亡人数比值,以评估不平等状况。结果:在基线情况下,非洲地区与RSV相关的ALRI发病率最高(117.4每1000人年,95%不确定性范围,UR:60.0–229.8),且RSV归因死亡率最高(0.97每1000人年,95% UR:0.76–1.31),但RSV相关ALRI住院率最低(12.6每1000人年;95% UR:7.5–21.3);东地中海地区住院率最高(29.9每1000人年,95% UR:14.2–63.2)。当进一步按国家收入水平细分上述估计时,RSV相关ALRI发病率、住院率和RSV归因死亡率的区域差异依然存在。截至2025年6月,尼塞韦单抗(尼塞韦单抗)和母体RSVpreF(疫苗)已在54和64个国家获得许可,其中16和12个国家将其纳入国家免疫计划。根据2025年6月产品使用情景,全球每年预计分别接种4,641,000剂尼塞韦单抗和1,955,000剂RSVpreF。这两种产品的联合使用预计每年可避免91,000(95% UR:75,000–118,000)例RSV相关ALRI住院病例和300(95% UR:210–470)例RSV归因死亡,分别对应全球住院病例和死亡的3.7%(95% UR:2.7–4.9)和0.4%(95% UR:0.3–0.7)。大约90%的避免住院病例和超过70%的避免死亡发生在高收入国家(分别为81,000 [95% UR: 66,000–108,000] 和 220 [95% UR: 140–390]),分别对应住院病例和死亡的减少33.2%(95% UR 31.0–35.9)和29.1%(95% UR 22.6–35.2)。相比之下,中等收入国家的住院病例和死亡的相对减少不到5%,而低收入国家预计没有减少。在没有实施的情景下,全球RSV归因总体死亡率存在显著不平等,RSV归因死亡的Q5-Q1比值估计为18.3(95% UR:11.7–27.5)。2025年6月产品使用情景可能与全球不平等的轻微增加相关,RSV归因死亡的Q5-Q1比值上升至20.8(95% UR:13.0–31.7)。解释:2019年全球RSV负担在不同地区和收入水平之间存在显著差异,非洲地区RSV相关ALRI发病率和RSV归因死亡率最高,但住院率最低。目前新型RSV预防产品的实施,特别是在高收入国家广泛许可和使用,而在LMICs,尤其是非洲地区缺乏可及性,预计只会对全球婴幼儿RSV疾病负担产生适度的减少。关键的是,这些产品的不平等可及性可能会加剧现有RSV负担的不平等。这些发现强调了在LMICs加速婴幼儿RSV免疫计划引入和扩大规模的迫切需求。资助:世界卫生组织和中国国家自然科学基金(82473692)。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估在实施新型预防产品前后的婴儿呼吸道合胞病毒疾病负担的区域不平等状况,解决低收入和中等收入国家(LMICs)中疾病负担不均衡的问题。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究重新分析了2019年全球呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)在婴儿中的疾病负担数据,按世界卫生组织地区和世界银行收入分类进行划分,并使用广义线性混合效应模型,预测了新型RSV预防产品的2025年6月前影响。
analysis_zh.methods: 通用线性混合效应模型被用于重新分析之前全球呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)在婴儿中的疾病负担数据集,并开发了一个静态确定性模型,以预测在两种情景下新型RSV预防产品的影响力:无实施情景和2025年6月产品使用情景。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在基线时,非洲地区在呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)相关急性下呼吸道感染(ALRI)和死亡病例的发病率和死亡率方面最高,而东地中海地区则具有最高的医院入院率。新型预防性产品的实施预计每年可避免91,000例RSV相关ALRI住院病例和300例RSV归因死亡,其中90%的避免住院病例和超过70%的避免死亡病例发生在高收入国家。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究发现,目前新型呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)预防产品的实施预计只会对全球婴儿RSV疾病负担产生适度的减少,可能会加剧现有RSV 死亡率负担的不平等状况。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现强调了在低收入和中等收入国家(LMICs),特别是非洲地区,亟需采取有针对性的策略,以加快婴幼儿呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)疫苗接种计划的引入和推广,从而减少该地区RSV疾病负担的不平等。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到依赖静态确定性模型和假设各国实施率一致的限制,这可能无法准确反映现实世界的情况。证据强度为中等。

Newsletter Videos Podcasts Contact Us Our Office General Enquiries Media Enquiries NMC Enquiries Disease Index Search Close End of the 2026 respiratory syncytial virus season 28 September , 2026 The 2026 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) season has ended. RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) in young children and can cause severe illness in infants. It is highly contagious, spreads primarily through respiratory droplets, and reinfections can occur. Risk factors for severe RSV-associated disease include prematurity, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease of prematurity, neurological conditions, immunodeficiency, lack of breastfeeding, HIV infection or exposure, and age under 6 months. Over the past decade, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic years 2020 and 2021, the RSV season in South Africa has typically begun around mid-February, with onset ranging from late January to late February. During the past 2 years, the start of the season was delayed compared to previous seasons. The 2026 season began in week 11 (week starting 9 March 2026), when the RSV detection rate among children aged <5 years enrolled in inpatient pneumonia surveillance at public hospitals exceeded the seasonal threshold and was sustained above the threshold for two consecutive weeks (Figure 1). RSV activity subsequently increased and peaked in week 25 (week starting 15 June 2026) at the moderate activity level, with the season ending in week 34 (week starting 17 August 2026). Message to clinicians Although the 2026 RSV season has ended, sporadic RSV infections may continue to occur outside the defined seasonal period. Clinicians should therefore continue to consider RSV in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with respiratory illness, particularly young infants and children at increased risk of severe disease. Prevention of RSV Measures to reduce the spread of RSV and other respiratory viruses remain important throughout the year, even after the defined RSV season has ended. These include avoiding close contact with people who are ill, regular handwashing, avoiding touching the mouth, eyes and nose, and covering coughs and sneezes appropriately. Individuals experiencing respiratory symptoms should stay at home where possible to reduce transmission to others. During the RSV season, additional RSV-specific preventive options are available for groups at increased risk of severe disease. Palivizumab, which requires monthly administration during the RSV season, has been available in South Africa for some time, although its high cost may limit its use. Long-acting monoclonal antibodies are also available in the private sector for infant protection, while maternal RSV vaccination is available in the private sector to protect infants. Introduction of maternal RSV vaccination into the public sector is being considered but is not currently available. As these interventions are targeted to specific groups and, in some instances, timed in relation to the RSV season, general measures to reduce respiratory virus transmission remain important throughout the year. Where to find updated data Weekly reports documenting respiratory pathogen circulation in South Africa, including influenza, RSV, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and Bordetella pertussis, are available here. Statements Blogs Newsletter Videos Podcasts Contact Us Our Office General Enquiries Media Enquiries NMC Enquiries Disease Index Search Close End of the 2026 respiratory syncytial virus season 28 September , 2026 The 2026 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) season has ended. RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) in young children and can cause severe illness in infants. It is highly contagious, spreads primarily through respiratory droplets, and reinfections can occur. Risk factors for severe RSV-associated disease include prematurity, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease of prematurity, neurological conditions, immunodeficiency, lack of breastfeeding, HIV infection or exposure, and age under 6 months. Over the past decade, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic years 2020 and 2021, the RSV season in South Africa has typically begun around mid-February, with onset ranging from late January to late February. During the past 2 years, the start of the season was delayed compared to previous seasons. The 2026 season began in week 11 (week starting 9 March 2026), when the RSV detection rate among children aged <5 years enrolled in inpatient pneumonia surveillance at public hospitals exceeded the seasonal threshold and was sustained above the threshold for two consecutive weeks (Figure 1). RSV activity subsequently increased and peaked in week 25 (week starting 15 June 2026) at the moderate activity level, with the season ending in week 34 (week starting 17 August 2026). Message to clinicians Although the 2026 RSV season has ended, sporadic RSV infections may continue to occur outside the defined seasonal period. Clinicians should therefore continue to consider RSV in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with respiratory illness, particularly young infants and children at increased risk of severe disease. Prevention of RSV Measures to reduce the spread of RSV and other respiratory viruses remain important throughout the year, even after the defined RSV season has ended. These include avoiding close contact with people who are ill, regular handwashing, avoiding touching the mouth, eyes and nose, and covering coughs and sneezes appropriately. Individuals experiencing respiratory symptoms should stay at home where possible to reduce transmission to others. During the RSV season, additional RSV-specific preventive options are available for groups at increased risk of severe disease. Palivizumab, which requires monthly administration during the RSV season, has been available in South Africa for some time, although its high cost may limit its use. Long-acting monoclonal antibodies are also available in the private sector for infant protection, while maternal RSV vaccination is available in the private sector to protect infants. Introduction of maternal RSV vaccination into the public sector is being considered but is not currently available. As these interventions are targeted to specific groups and, in some instances, timed in relation to the RSV season, general measures to reduce respiratory virus transmission remain important throughout the year. Where to find updated data Weekly reports documenting respiratory pathogen circulation in South Africa, including influenza, RSV, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and Bordetella pertussis, are available here. The NICD also highlights the importance of general measures to reduce respiratory virus transmission year-round.

news.source_body_en: The National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD) has announced the end of the 2026 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) season, which began in week 11 (9 March 2026) and peaked in week 25 (15 June 2026). The season concluded in week 34 (17 August 2026), with RSV activity remaining moderate. The event was reported based on data from children aged <5 years in public hospitals participating in inpatient pneumonia surveillance. RSV is a significant cause of bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infections in young children, particularly infants, and can lead to severe illness in those with risk factors such as prematurity or immunodeficiency. Clinicians are urged to remain vigilant and consider RSV in the differential diagnosis of respiratory symptoms, especially in high-risk patients. Prevention measures, including avoiding close contact with sick individuals, regular handwashing, and covering coughs and sneezes, are emphasized. RSV-specific preventive options, such as palivizumab, are available for at-risk groups, though their high cost may limit use. The NICD also highlights the importance of general measures to reduce respiratory virus transmission year-round.
news.content_zh: 国家传染病研究所(NICD)宣布2026年呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)季已结束,该季始于第11周(2026年3月9日),并在第25周(2026年6月15日)达到高峰,于第34周(2026年8月17日)结束,RSV活动水平保持中等。该事件基于参与住院肺炎监测的公共医院中<5岁儿童的数据进行报告。RSV是导致年轻儿童(尤其是婴儿)毛细支气管炎和下呼吸道感染的重要原因,且可能在有早产、先天性心脏病或免疫缺陷等风险因素的患者中引发严重疾病。临床医生被敦促保持警惕,并在出现呼吸道症状的患者中考虑RSV作为鉴别诊断,特别是高风险婴儿。预防措施,包括避免与生病的人密切接触、定期洗手以及遮掩咳嗽和打喷嚏,被强调。针对高风险人群,RSV特异性预防选项如palivizumab可供使用,但其高昂的成本可能限制其应用。此外,NICD还强调了全年减少呼吸道病毒传播的一般措施的重要性。

news.content_title: Low RSV Vaccine Coverage Leaves Seniors at Risk
news.content: Medscape AI News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Medscape News CanadaFeatures Low RSV Vaccine Coverage Leaves Seniors at Risk Evra Taylor September 29, 2026 Respiratory virus season will begin soon in Canada, but recent government data indicate low respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine coverage among older Canadians. Only 34% of Canadians aged 75 years or older reported being vaccinated, along with only 21% of those aged 60-74 years with chronic conditions. A recent update from the National Advisory Committee on Immunization (NACI) strongly recommends vaccination for everyone aged 75 years or older and for patients aged 65-74 years who are at increased risk for severe disease. But the provinces are free to determine which vaccination programs to fund. RSV is a common respiratory virus that can cause serious complications, including hospitalization, ICU admission, and death, in older adults and patients with certain medical conditions. Historically, RSV has been seen as a disease affecting children younger than 24 months. This is because it was first recognized in the pediatric population, and most of the surveillance, prevention, and public awareness were focused on children. But globally, the disease is associated with roughly 336,000 hospitalizations and 14,000 in-hospital deaths each year in adults aged 65 years or older, according to a systematic review. The first RSV vaccine for patients aged 60 years or older received Health Canada approval in August 2023. Older Adults and RSV Risk “For older adults, particularly those with underlying health conditions, RSV is not simply a bad cold,” Ian Culbert, executive director of the Canadian Public Health Association, told Medscape News Canada. “It can cause pneumonia, exacerbate chronic heart and lung disease, lead to hospitalization and intensive care stays, and even result in death. We definitely need to broaden the way we talk about RSV. It certainly remains an important pediatric infection, but it’s also an important cause of serious illness in older adults and adults with certain chronic conditions.” RSV causes 5%-8% of symptomatic respiratory infections in adults aged 60 years or older. Patients in their eighties have particularly high rates of infection, and the virus becomes more prevalent with age, Culbert explained. The benefits of the vaccine for older adults are clear, according to Isaac Bogoch, MD, infectious disease specialist at Toronto General Hospital in Toronto. “The emerging data for the RSV vaccine deployed in older Canadians appear to be pretty darn good,” Bogoch told Medscape News Canada. “Real-world experience is emulating the trials being conducted, and the vaccine is reducing the risk of hospitalization with ICU stays. The nice thing about this vaccine is its very long lifespan: It probably has decent efficacy for two or even more seasons,” he added. When patients are admitted to the hospital for a respiratory illness such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation, heart failure, or community-acquired pneumonia, it’s an opportune time to discuss their risk factors for severe infection and protective measures that will reduce their risk for further hospitalizations related to RSV or other infections, Bogoch noted. Lack of Provincial Coverage Affects Access Clinicians play an important role in talking to older patients about RSV vaccination. In surveys, patients often say that they weren’t told about the vaccination option. But a recommendation from a clinician doesn’t necessarily translate into access to the vaccine. Most provinces and territories have limited or no universal public funding for routine adult RSV vaccination outside of specific high-risk groups. Despite the NACI recommendation, public funding varies wildly across various regions and residential settings, and coverage is nuanced. British Columbia, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island cover adults aged 75 years or older, for example. British Columbia has a free, time-limited vaccination program starting in fall 2026 for Indigenous patients aged 60 years or older. Alberta pays for the vaccine for those aged 70 years or older; residents of continuing care or senior supportive living aged 60 years or older; and First Nations, Métis, and Inuit patients aged 60 years or older. “The problem is how sick people can get and the duration of the illness. It affects their lifespan going forward,” said Jobin Varughese, MD, family physician and assistant dean of primary care education at Toronto Metropolitan University in Toronto. “The people most at risk are those with COPD, bronchitis, emphysema, or even frequent viral colds — so is anyone over age 60 years in a long-term care facility or retirement setting where they’re at close quarters with other elderly patients.” With age, lungs lose a lot of their plasticity and their ability to fight off infection. With a decreased immune response, it’s critical that seniors be vaccinated, Varughese explained. “A person’s access to a recommended vaccine should not depend so heavily on where they live in Canada. By investing in vaccines, we can take the pressure off hospitals and emergency rooms, especially during respiratory virus season,” concluded Culbert. Culbert, Bogoch, and Varughese reported having no relevant financial relationships. Evra Taylor is a widely published freelance medical writer and reporter with 20 years’ experience covering a broad range of therapeutic sectors, including family health, cardiology, psychiatry, ophthalmology, and dermatology. Prepping for Fall: It Is Time for Everyone to Get Their Annual Respiratory Virus Vaccines PR Newswire Tue, September 29, 2026 at 6:08 AM EDT 4 min read American Lung Association launches campaign to educate people living with lung disease and other risk factors about critical vaccines CHICAGO, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- September marks the unofficial start of the respiratory virus season and the potential for related spikes in influenza (flu), COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), so the American Lung Association is urging everyone to talk to their healthcare provider now about recommended vaccines to protect themselves from severe illness, complications and hospitalization. American Lung Association logo Each year, respiratory viruses cause hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations, which significantly impact a person's work, school and family time. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Respiratory Virus Hospitalization Surveillance Network: There was an estimated 32 million illnesses, 390,000 hospitalizations and 24,000 deaths during the 2025-2026 influenza season. From October 1, 2025, through July 18, 2026, as many as 2.3 million COVID-19 outpatient visits and 240,000 COVID-19 hospitalizations. From October 1, 2025, through June 6, 2026, there have been an estimated 2.8 million RSV outpatient visits and as many as 340,000 RSV hospitalizations. "Fortunately, vaccines are available and effective in keeping people healthy, active and out of the hospital. Vaccines are especially important for the 35 million individuals in the United States with lung disease, like asthma or COPD, because respiratory infections can worsen existing lung disease symptoms," said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. "As families look ahead to the winter and the holiday season, the best thing they can do to protect their health is to make sure everyone is up to date on their recommended vaccinations." The Lung Association encourages individuals to speak to a healthcare provider about receiving the following recommended vaccines to prevent severe illness this respiratory virus season, which typically peaks from October through March: Flu: Everyone ages six months and older is recommended to get a flu shot annually. COVID-19: Everyone six months and older or their caregiver should discuss COVID-19 vaccination with a healthcare provider. RSV: Adults ages 50 to 74 who are at an increased risk of developing severe RSV illness, like adults living with chronic lung or heart disease, and all adults ages 75 or older are recommended to get a single RSV vaccine if they have not received one previously. Additional doses are not recommended at this time. Story Continues For the millions of people in the U.S. living with asthma, respiratory viruses like flu, COVID-19 and RSV can place added stress on the lungs even when asthma is mild or well controlled. Respiratory viruses are the leading cause of asthma flare-ups, or exacerbations, accounting for up to 80% of asthma attacks, according to the CDC. Adults with asthma are more likely to develop pneumonia after getting sick with the flu than people who do not have asthma. In addition, respiratory illnesses pose a serious risk to individuals with lung cancer because their body, including their lungs, is already vulnerable from cancer and its treatments, such as radiation and surgery. Many people with lung cancer may have weakened immune systems, meaning that they may not be able to easily fight off viral infections which can quickly become severe and lead to complications like pneumonia or hospitalization. People living with COPD are also at increased risk of serious complications from respiratory viruses. Respiratory infections are a leading cause of COPD flare-ups, or exacerbations, which can worsen symptoms such as shortness of breath, coughing and excess mucus production. These flare-ups can take weeks or longer to recover from and increase the risk of hospitalization and other serious complications. Educating adults about vaccine-preventable disease is essential to reducing severe illness and hospitalizations. The Lung Association is working to achieve this by: Sharing trusted, science-based information about vaccine safety, effectiveness and accessibility. Raising awareness about surveillance trends during the 2026-2027 fall and winter respiratory virus season. Educating people about factors that increase risk for severe symptoms and hospitalization from respiratory viruses, especially resources for people living with lung disease and lung cancer. Encouraging people to talk to their healthcare provider about risk factors for severe respiratory illness and recommended prevention strategies. For more information on vaccines that protect against infectious respiratory diseases, visit Lung.org/vaccines. Support for this campaign is provided by Moderna. About the American Lung Association The American Lung Association is the leading organization working to save lives by improving lung health and preventing lung disease through education, advocacy and research. The work of the American Lung Association is focused on four strategic imperatives: to defeat lung cancer; to champion clean air for all; to improve the quality of life for those with lung disease and their families; and to create a tobacco-free future. For more information about the American Lung Association, which has a 4-star rating from Charity Navigator and is a Platinum-Level GuideStar Member, call 1-800-LUNGUSA (1-800-586-4872) or visit: Lung.org. To support the work of the American Lung Association, find a local event at Lung.org/events or donate today at Lung.org/donate. From October 1, 2025, through June 6, 2026, there have been an estimated 2.8 million RSV outpatient visits and as many as 340,000 RSV hospitalizations. "Fortunately, vaccines are available and effective in keeping people healthy, active and out of the hospital. Vaccines are especially important for the 35 million individuals in the United States with lung disease, like asthma or COPD, because respiratory infections can worsen existing lung disease symptoms," said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. "As families look ahead to the winter and the holiday season, the best thing they can do to protect their health is to make sure everyone is up to date on their recommended vaccinations." The Lung Association encourages individuals to speak to a healthcare provider about receiving the following recommended vaccines to prevent severe illness this respiratory virus season, which typically peaks from October through March: Flu: Everyone ages six months and older is recommended to get a flu shot annually. COVID-19: Everyone six months and older or their caregiver should discuss COVID-19 vaccination with a healthcare provider. RSV: Adults ages 50 to 74 who are at an increased risk of developing severe RSV illness, like adults living with chronic lung or heart disease, and all adults ages 75 or older are recommended to get a single RSV vaccine if they have not received one previously. Additional doses are not recommended at this time. Story Continues For the millions of people in the U.S. living with asthma, respiratory viruses like flu, COVID-19 and RSV can place added stress on the lungs even when asthma is mild or well controlled. Respiratory viruses are the leading cause of asthma flare-ups, or exacerbations, accounting for up to 80% of asthma attacks, according to the CDC. Adults with asthma are more likely to develop pneumonia after getting sick with the flu than people who do not have asthma. In addition, respiratory illnesses pose a serious risk to individuals with lung cancer because their body, including their lungs, is already vulnerable from cancer and its treatments, such as radiation and surgery. Many people with lung cancer may have weakened immune systems, meaning that they may not be able to easily fight off viral infections which can quickly become severe and lead to complications like pneumonia or hospitalization. People living with COPD are also at increased risk of serious complications from respiratory viruses. Respiratory infections are a leading cause of COPD flare-ups, or exacerbations, which can worsen symptoms such as shortness of breath, coughing and excess mucus production. These flare-ups can take weeks or longer to recover from and increase the risk of hospitalization and other serious complications. Educating adults about vaccine-preventable disease is essential to reducing severe illness and hospitalizations. The Lung Association is working to achieve this by: Sharing trusted, science-based information about vaccine safety, effectiveness and accessibility. Raising awareness about surveillance trends during the 2026-2027 fall and winter respiratory virus season. Educating people about factors that increase risk for severe symptoms and hospitalization from respiratory viruses, especially resources for people living with lung disease and lung cancer. Encouraging people to talk to their healthcare provider about risk factors for severe respiratory illness and recommended prevention strategies. For more information on vaccines that protect against infectious respiratory diseases, visit Lung.org/vaccines. Support for this campaign is provided by Moderna. About the American Lung Association The American Lung Association is the leading organization working to save lives by improving lung health and preventing lung disease through education, advocacy and research. The work of the American Lung Association is focused on four strategic imperatives: to defeat lung cancer; to champion clean air for all; to improve the quality of life for those with lung disease and their families; and to create a tobacco-free future. For more information about the American Lung Association, which has a 4-star rating from Charity Navigator and is a Platinum-Level GuideStar Member, call 1-800-LUNGUSA (1-800-586-4872) or visit: Lung.org. To support the work of the American Lung Association, find a local event at Lung.org/events or donate today at Lung.org/donate. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Washington State University News and Information for Faculty, Staff, and the WSU Community WSU Insider Go to WSU Twitter Go to WSU Facebook Go to WSU Linkedin Menu Quicklinks / Search Subscribe Close Quick Links Close Search Choose to search this site or all WSU sites news.wsu.edu All wsu.edu Quick Links Announcements Press Releases News Categories Arts & Culture Awards & Achievements Benefits & Training Business & Economics Campus & Community Food & Agriculture Health & Medicine Politics & Society Reports & Updates Science & Technology University Affairs Veterinary Medicine Close Menu Close Menu Search/Quicklinks News News Categories Arts & Culture Awards & Achievements Benefits & Training Business & Economics Campus & Community Food & Agriculture Health & Medicine Politics & Society Reports & Updates Science & Technology University Affairs Veterinary Medicine Announcements Contact Us For Journalists Press Releases Institutional Data Quick Facts Subscribe Search News News Categories Arts & Culture Awards & Achievements Benefits & Training Business & Economics Campus & Community Food & Agriculture Health & Medicine Politics & Society Reports & Updates Science & Technology University Affairs Veterinary Medicine Close Menu Announcements Contact Us For Journalists Press Releases Institutional Data Quick Facts Close Menu Subscribe Search NIH awards WSU researcher $3M to study inflammatory response during virus infection September 29, 2026 By Devin Rokyta, College of Veterinary Medicine Share on Twitter Share on FaceBook Share on Linkedin share with email share with link WSU researchers are studying how the immune response to RSV can cause lung inflammation and damage (photo by wildpixel on iStock). Washington State University researcher Santanu Bose has been awarded a $3.04 million grant from the National Institutes of Health for research that could lead to new treatment options for human respiratory syncytial virus, commonly known as RSV, and other respiratory viral infections. RSV is a leading cause of respiratory illness worldwide, particularly among infants, young children and people with weakened immune systems. It can cause pneumonia and bronchiolitis, and infections early in life have been linked to an increased risk of developing chronic respiratory conditions such as asthma. The five-year grant will support a project aimed at understanding how the body’s own immune response to RSV can cause significant lung damage leading to inflammatory diseases like pneumonia and how that process may be blocked by therapeutic agents to combat lung disease. The project will be conducted in collaboration with Sid Balachandran, director of the Center for Immunology at Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia. Santanu Bose “Our immune response to RSV is a double-edged sword,” said Bose, a professor of immunology and infectious diseases in WSU’s College of Veterinary Medicine. “We’re trying to understand why the immune response sometimes goes too far and ends up damaging the lungs by inflammation. In many ways, the body could eliminate the virus with a regulated inflammatory response, but instead it responds with excessive inflammation, , which ends up harming the host.” When RSV infects cells, the body’s immune system responds with a process known as lytic cell death, also known as necroptosis and pyroptosis, in which infected cells rupture and release their contents into surrounding tissue. While the response can help fight infection, it can also lead to excessive inflammation that damages the lungs and contributes to diseases such as pneumonia. Bose’s laboratory has already identified a key immune-signaling pathway involved in triggering “damaging” lytic cell death during RSV infection. The new grant will help provide a better understanding of how this cellular immune pathway works and explore therapeutic ways to block the harmful cellular signals that drive the damaging inflammatory response leading to lung disease. This may result in development of effective host-directed therapeutics to combat viral pneumonia. Although the grant is focused on RSV, Bose said the work could have broader implications for other viruses that are related to RSV. “Often it’s not the virus itself that causes the greatest damage,” Bose said. “A lot of the harm comes from the body’s response to infection. If we can learn how to control that response, it could help us develop new treatments not only for RSV but for other serious respiratory and non-respiratory viral infections as well.” Next Story Anjan Bose elected International Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering September 29, 2026 A globally recognized expert in electric power systems, Bose has helped shape many of the technologies and analytical tools that underpin today’s electric grid. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, September 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health RSV Genomes Reveal Viral Diversification in Lombardy After Nirsevimab Rollout by Bioengineer September 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, remains one of the most consequential respiratory pathogens of early childhood, and the arrival of long-acting monoclonal antibody prophylaxis has transformed the landscape of infant protection. A new genomic surveillance study from Lombardy, Italy, published in Genome Medicine, offers one of the most detailed pictures yet of how circulating RSV strains have evolved across the very seasons in which nirsevimab was introduced into routine clinical practice. By sequencing whole viral genomes from patients infected before and after the prophylaxis program began, researchers tracked clade turnover, the emergence of large phylogenetic clusters, and the appearance of mutations at sites known to mediate resistance to monoclonal antibodies and antiviral small molecules. The research team collected RSV-positive upper respiratory tract samples from patients who tested positive between October 2023 and March 2025, spanning two consecutive seasons that straddled the deployment of nirsevimab. Whole viral genomes were recovered using an amplicon-based sequencing protocol carried out on Illumina platforms, with assemblies generated through a consensus-building pipeline known as vcf-consensus-builder. This approach allowed the investigators to capture near-complete genomes from a substantial fraction of positive samples, providing the resolution needed to place each virus within a fine-grained phylogenetic framework and to examine amino acid variation in the proteins most relevant to prevention and treatment. In total, the study retrieved 302 RSV genome sequences, with 129 derived from the 2023–2024 season and 173 from the 2024–2025 season. The clinical composition of the cohort reflects the burden of RSV disease in the region: most infections occurred in infants aged one year or younger, who accounted for 56.0 percent of cases, and males made up 57.3 percent of the sampled population. Lower respiratory tract infections were documented in 72.7 percent of cases, 67.2 percent of patients required hospitalization, and 15.0 percent were admitted to an intensive care unit. Notably, the dataset included 17 nirsevimab breakthrough infections, cases in which infants who had received the monoclonal antibody nonetheless developed symptomatic RSV disease. Discover more genomes genome respiratory syncytial virus Respiratory syncytial virus genomic Phylogenetic analysis using maximum-likelihood methods implemented in IQ-TREE, with a GTR plus F, invariant sites, and gamma model of substitution, assigned the circulating viruses to established clades within the two major RSV subgroups. The most frequently detected clades were A.D.3, representing 26.8 percent of sequences, and B.D.E.1, representing 20.2 percent, followed by A.D.1.2 at 17.5 percent and A.D.5.2 at 14.2 percent. This distribution confirms that multiple lineages of both RSV-A and RSV-B co-circulated in Lombardy throughout the study period, with no single clade achieving complete dominance across the two seasons. Beyond clade assignment, the researchers applied Bayesian coalescent methods under a constant population size prior and a strict molecular clock to define what they termed large phylogenetic clusters, or LPCs. These were groups of more than ten sequences supported by a posterior probability of one, indicating tightly linked transmission chains or rapidly expanding lineages. Four such clusters were identified, and two of them proved particularly striking: a cluster of 56 A.D.3 strains and another of 17 A.D.1.2 strains were detected exclusively in the 2024–2025 season, the first season of routine nirsevimab use. The emergence of season-specific clusters suggests that new viral lineages established themselves in the population after the prophylaxis program began. A central concern of the study was the monitoring of mutations associated with resistance to the preventive and therapeutic agents now deployed against RSV. The fusion protein, or F, is the target of the monoclonal antibodies palivizumab, nirsevimab, and clesrovimab, while the nucleoprotein, or N, is the target of the small-molecule inhibitor zelicapavir. Resistance-associated mutations were identified in two samples from the 2023–2024 season and two from the 2024–2025 season. These included K272E in an A.D.5.3 strain and N262Y in an A.D.3 strain, both associated with reduced susceptibility to palivizumab, and N208D in a B.D.E.1 strain as well as the combination of K68I and L204S in a B.D.E.1 nirsevimab breakthrough infection, mutations linked to nirsevimab resistance. Among the 17 nirsevimab breakthrough infections, the investigators also detected the S213R substitution at antigenic site Ø of the F protein in an A.D.1.2 sample. Site Ø is the principal binding site for nirsevimab, and changes at this region can diminish antibody binding. By contrast, no mutations conferring resistance to clesrovimab, a newer monoclonal antibody that binds a different region of F, were detected during the study. However, four substitutions were observed at the clesrovimab binding site: K433R in a B.D.4.1.1 strain, C439R in an A.D.1.2 strain, N437S in an A.D.5.2 strain, and N444S in an A.D.3 strain, with three of the four appearing during the 2024–2025 season. These variants were not classified as resistance mutations, but their presence at a pharmacologically critical epitope warrants continued attention. Discover more Infectious Diseases Biological Sciences Genetics Health Conditions infection The nucleoprotein analysis likewise revealed signals relevant to antiviral therapy. The I129M substitution in the N protein, which is associated with resistance to zelicapavir, was detected in a B.D.E.1 sample from the 2024–2025 season at an intrapatient relative abundance of 0.05, indicating that the variant existed as a minor species within the quasispecies of that infection rather than as the dominant viral population. Such low-frequency variants are typically invisible to conventional diagnostic assays but can be resolved by deep sequencing, and their detection underscores the value of high-resolution genomic surveillance in identifying resistance determinants before they become established at the population level. Multivariable analysis comparing the two seasons revealed several statistically significant differences associated with the 2024–2025 period. That season was characterized by an increased number of sequences belonging to large phylogenetic clusters, greater amino acid variability at antigenic site Ø of the F protein, and higher Ct values on diagnostic testing, which correspond to lower viral loads in respiratory samples. Hospital intensive care unit admissions were also fewer in the second season. While the observational design of the study precludes drawing direct causal links between nirsevimab deployment and these shifts, the concurrence of prophylaxis introduction with reduced disease severity, altered viral population structure, and expanded F protein variability provides a compelling rationale for sustained monitoring. The overall message from the Lombardy surveillance program is one of cautious reassurance combined with vigilance. Nirsevimab breakthrough infections remained rare relative to the scale of the prophylaxis campaign, and bona fide resistance mutations were detected in only a handful of samples across two seasons. At the same time, the virus is demonstrably diversifying, with season-specific phylogenetic clusters and accumulating variation at antibody binding sites on the F protein. As monoclonal antibodies and vaccines become mainstays of RSV prevention worldwide, the Lombardy experience illustrates how whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic clustering, and mutation-level analysis can be woven into routine public health practice, ensuring that shifts in viral evolution are detected early enough to inform and adjust prophylaxis strategies before they compromise protection of the most vulnerable patients. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Download the AppGet your news faster with our mobile experience Install News Weather Sports Features Newsletter Sign Up Watch Live Now 73° Wed 74° Thu 77° Sign In or Create Account Live1 Sponsored Baby Your Baby- Flu and RSV Immunizations to Protect Babies from Serious Illness by Intermountain Health Mon, September 28, 2026 at 10:38 AM Play/Pause Video Quality Speed0.25x0.5xnormal1.5x2x Audio Track Audio Quality Subtitlesopen Font sizedefault50%75%100%150%200%300%400% Font styledefaultitalicbold Font familydefaultmonospaced serifproportional serifmonospaced sans serifproportional sans serifcasualcursivesmall capital Font colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Font opacitydefault100%75%50%25% Character edgedefaultraiseddepresseduniformdrop shadowed Character edge colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Background colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Background opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0% Window colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Window opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0% BackReset 00:01 00:00 PlayMute Picture-in-PictureApple AirPlayGoogle CastVRSettingsFullscreen Replay logo Baby Your Baby- RSV and Flu 0Comment Share topics: RSV Influenza Immunization Intermountain Health Utah Nirsevimb Maternal vaccination Hospitalization Fall brings the perfect time to remind everyone to protect their baby from flu and RSV, which are circulating in Utah communities now and already causing some children to be hospitalized. “RSV immunization and influenza vaccine are the simplest, most effective ways to protect young children against these diseases, which can lead to serious difficulty breathing, hospitalization and in rare cases, death of young children and other at-risk populations,” said Diane Liu, MD. Seasonal influenza or flu can cause a variety of symptoms from mild tiredness, cough and chills to more severe symptoms such as fever, body aches, nausea, and difficulty breathing. These symptoms can keep kids in bed for days to a week, and in some cases, require a hospital stay. RSV, or Respiratory Syncytial Virus, is a highly contagious virus that causes bronchiolitis, a lung inflammation that can result in severe illness in infants. Every year in the United States, RSV is linked to thousands of hospitalizations, hundreds of deaths, and millions of clinic visits in children under the age of five. Infants and young children with RSV or flu are at risk for serious illness because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. Babies born prematurely and young children with heart and lung conditions are especially at risk. Also, unlike older kids and adults, young babies don’t know how to clear their airways effectively. Powered By 10 Sec Heavy rain floods Salem street after six-hour downpour Next Stay The best way to mitigate these risks is with RSV and flu immunizations. Intermountain Health recommends flu vaccine for everyone ages 6 months and older. It also recommends RSV protection for babies in one of the following ways: Expectant moms in their third trimester of pregnancy (between 32-36 weeks gestation) can get the maternal RSV shot and pass the antibodies to their babies to help protect them during their first few vulnerable months of life. Infants whose moms didn’t receive the shot during pregnancy, can get Nirsevimb monoclonal antibody in a shot at birth from October through March, as well as those born outside of RSV season (between April and September). If a mother did not receive the maternal shot during her 3rd trimester, then her baby is eligible from birth until age 8 months. Toddlers and infants under the age of 19 months may be eligible if they have a medical condition that warrants immunization. Recently, Utah babies with RSV protection were nine timeslesslikely to be hospitalized, and five times less likely to need intensive care to help them breatheif they were hospitalized, than babieswithoutRSV protection, Intermountain Health found. If you have any questions about immunizations, Intermountain recommends talking to your health care provider so you get the information you need to make the best decision for your child. supplementary_news.content_title: Experts urge residents to get fall respiratory shots
supplementary_news.content: News Sports Opinions Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL Experts urge residents to get fall respiratory shots Monique Calello Staunton News Leader Sept. 29, 2026, 4:30 a.m. ET As respiratory illness season begins this fall, the Central Shenandoah Health District is encouraging residents to get vaccinated against influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus, commonly known as RSV. According to the health district, vaccines remain the best protection against severe illness caused by respiratory viruses. Residents should consult their health care providers to determine which 2026-27 seasonal vaccines are appropriate for them. "These can be serious illnesses and should not be taken lightly," said Marsha Rodeffer, nursing manager for the Central Shenandoah Health District. "Flu deaths can climb into the tens of thousands each year. With effective vaccines available, taking a chance on getting sick is never worth the risk." Who should get a flu vaccine this season? The Central Shenandoah Health District recommends that everyone 6 months and older, with rare exceptions, receive an influenza vaccine each season. According to the health district, the ideal time to receive a flu vaccine is by the end of October, but vaccination can still provide protection as long as flu viruses continue circulating. Flu activity typically begins increasing in October and can continue through May, often peaking in January or February. The updated flu vaccine protects against three strains of influenza virus, including the influenza A(H3N2) subclade K virus that circulated widely during the 2025-26 flu season, according to health officials. Who should get the updated COVID-19 vaccine? COVID-19 vaccines are available for everyone 6 months and older and are especially recommended for people at higher risk of severe illness, including older adults, infants and during pregnancy, according to the health district. The health district recommends that eligible individuals receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine because immunity from previous vaccination can decrease over time. Who should get an RSV vaccine or immunization? The Central Shenandoah Health District recommends a single dose of an RSV vaccine for all adults 75 and older. Adults ages 50 to 74 with certain underlying health conditions should consult their health care providers to determine whether an RSV vaccine is appropriate for them. According to the health district, adults 50 and older who previously received an RSV vaccine do not need another dose this season. Health officials also recommend that all infants be protected from severe RSV illness through one of two immunization options. A maternal RSV vaccine can be administered during pregnancy, or a monoclonal antibody can be given to an infant after birth. According to the health district, these immunization options significantly reduce the risk of RSV-related hospitalization during a child's first RSV season. People who are pregnant and parents of newborns are encouraged to discuss RSV immunization options with their health care providers. For more information, contact the Staunton-Augusta Health Department at cshdinfo@vdh.virginia.gov or visit the Virginia Department of Health's respiratory illness webpage. Monique Calello covers health and business news for The News Leader. Reach her at mcalello@newsleader.com.
